title: Ideal gas law and units
objectives: Explain the particle basis of PV=nRT; choose consistent pressure, volume and temperature units; solve for one unknown and test whether the ideal model is appropriate.
difficulty: Beginner through application; final question is a challenge
instructions: Show the equation, substitution, arithmetic and units for numerical answers. Explain physical meaning. Use given constants. Retain intermediate digits and round final answers as requested; for unspecified precision, accept sensible rounding. Graphs and data are simulated educational models.

questions.prompt: A gas is at 22.0 °C. Give the unrounded Kelvin conversion used in PV=nRT. Explain why 22.0 is not the correct temperature input.
Which R is appropriate for P in kPa, V in L, n in mol and T in K? A. 8.314 kPa·L/(mol·K). B. 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) without any conversion. Explain.
A gas sample is compressed at constant T and n from 4.0 L to 2.0 L. Predict how its ideal-gas pressure changes and give the factor.
A gauge reads 30 kPa above local atmospheric pressure of 100 kPa. What pressure belongs in PV=nRT?
An ideal gas has n=0.150 mol, T=320 K and V=4.00 L. Use R=8.314 kPa·L/(mol·K). Find absolute pressure to three significant figures.
A gas occupies 6.00 L at 100 kPa absolute and 300 K. Use R=8.314 kPa·L/(mol·K). Find n to three significant figures.
A sealed rigid vessel contains ideal gas at 120 kPa absolute and 300 K. It cools to 270 K with no gas lost. Find the final pressure and name the two fixed quantities that justify the shortcut.

Challenge: A 2.00 g gas sample has molar mass 4.00 g/mol, temperature 27.0 °C and absolute pressure 100 kPa. Use R=8.314 kPa·L/(mol·K). Calculate volume and name one condition that could make the ideal model unreliable.
